video.title: This Business Makes Vending Machines Look Dumb

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Forest, a 34-year-old former Pepsi/Coke/Bang merchandiser and beverage brand rep. He bought a failed pastry route for $15k, grew it to about $800k a year and sold it in two parts for about $185k. He then moved to Billings, Montana and started a small-distributor business selling jerky, candy and novelty snacks to independent gas stations and grocery stores. He reports about 95 accounts, roughly $50k a month in sales, 30% net margin and one lost account. The takeaway is that a hands-on, relationship-based route business that merchandises and buys back unsold stock, using local products, net-10 customer terms and net-14 to net-30 supplier terms, can start with very little capital. It is physical, driving-heavy work, not agent-run.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; owner of Texas Snacks gas station business, wholesale and retail experience

speakers.name: Forest
speakers.description: Owner of Cough Tree Wholesale (name as transcribed), a snack and jerky distributor in Billings, Montana; ex-Pepsi/Coke/Bang merchandiser and former pastry route owner

ideas.name: Independent-store jerky and candy micro-distributor (merchandising route)
ideas.one_liner: Drive a route to independent gas stations, grocery and hardware stores every 14 days, selling jerky, candy and novelty snacks by the case, merchandising the shelf and buying back unsold stock.
ideas.business_model: Wholesale resale margin: buy from manufacturers, mark up 30-45%, sell by the case to stores on net-10 terms. No service fee.
ideas.customer: Independent gas stations, small grocery stores, hardware stores, lumber yards, liquor stores and auto parts stores, mostly rural; small regional chains (e.g. 8-store and 20-store accounts).
ideas.problem: Big wholesalers drop product and leave, with no upselling or relationship, no regional or local products, and store owners carry the mental load of ordering and forecasting inventory. Out-of-stocks and outdated stock are not bought back.
ideas.offer: Visit every other week, place the order, merchandise and rotate the shelf, take over whole sections (e.g. jerky), supply products the big wholesaler does not carry (especially local brands), buy back credits on unsold or outdated items, and supply free manufacturer racks and displays. Positioned as an addition to the store's existing wholesaler.

pricing.model: Per-case wholesale with 30-45% markup over cost, net-10 customer terms

price_points.unit: per delivery at best grocery store
price_points.label: best grocery account

price_points.unit: per jerky case (some cases over $100; about $30 profit)
price_points.label: case price

pricing.notes: Markup 30-45%, so the example $1,000 order yields about $350-400 gross profit. Net margin about 30% when owner-operated, about 20% if staff run it. Sells by the case only.

acquisition_channels.details: Walks into independent stores with the product in the truck or trailer, a price sheet and a fun one-pager, and offers to fetch the display on the spot. Re-visits non-buyers every other Tuesday; the second follow-up is usually when they say yes. Early close rate about 4 in 10.

quote.text: you give them the one pager that has some fun photos. And I always tell them like, "Hey, let me go grab the product now."
quote.speaker: Forest

acquisition_channels.details: Relationship-based; owners help other local businesses. Existing accounts and regional chains bring more stores (e.g. a 30-store owner, a 25-store regional account, a four-store chain asking him to bring in a brand).

Manufacturers want distributors; one jerky brand sent a salesman to open stores for him. Called competitor owners for market insight and brand intros. Used Google to find cool local or non-saturated brands and pitched them using a list of about 50 independent stores.
Used Google Maps and satellite or street view to find stores that look independent, ignoring fuel branding like Shell or BP, and built the route list from that.

ideas.delivery: Owner drives a pickup with an enclosed trailer (now a box truck) 10-12 stops a day, about 6-8 hours, in a radius of about 2.5 hours around Billings. He is salesperson, driver, merchandiser and order-taker. Monday is warehouse day: pallets are received by staff at a local storage facility and the family helps put away stock. Invoices are made in a cheap app and printed. Buy-backs are rare because he picks products himself.
unit_economics_claims: About $50k/month revenue from about 95 accounts at roughly $500/month each
Gross margin about 35-40%, net margin about 30% owner-operated
Warehouse about $1,400/month for 1,500 sq ft; earlier two storage units about $500/month
One account lost in about 16 months
Full route could gross about $800k/yr with a $50-70k/yr driver
tools: Local storage-facility warehouse with staff receiving
ideas.startup_cost: Very low: a first manufacturer order of about $2,500 on 14-day terms (free racks), a car or trailer, and a cheap invoice app. Claimed it can be started with almost no money.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About $20,000 in sales in the first month in Billings (claimed, per host)

acquisition.how: Door-to-door walk-in sales to store owners is in-person and relationship-based. Agents could help build target lists from Maps and manage follow-up schedules, but the selling is human.

onboarding.how: Setting up a store means a physical display install and a verbal agreement, with no contracts. Account records could be digitised.

delivery.how: Driving, carrying cases, merchandising shelves, receiving pallets and buy-backs are all physical work done every visit.

billing.how: Net-10 invoices from an app could be automated with accounting software and payment reminders. Stores currently pay by cheque or cash on the next visit.

support.how: Support is an owner relationship on the next visit; order changes could be handled by messaging but the model depends on face time.

uk_applicability.notes: Independent convenience stores, farm shops, garages and pubs exist in the UK, and cash-and-carry or van-sales models are established. The UK is much denser and smaller, so competition is higher and the large-radius rural advantage is less relevant. Food labelling, hygiene registration and shelf-life rules apply. Selling to stores is B2B, so PECR is not a barrier to visits, but cold email or call to sole traders needs care. Prices would be in GBP with local British brands.

risks: Competing wholesaler can undercut and steal an account (happened once)
Perishable or dated goods cause write-offs and buy-backs
Relationships are fragile and scaling needs staff
Heavy physical driving workload, weather (-20°C) and rural distance
Brands may limit territories or terms
Chain stores are hard to enter

ideas.name: Pastry/danish route distribution (Bone Appetit)
ideas.one_liner: Forest bought a failed pastry-distribution business for $15k, resold California bakery danishes and donuts to stores from a rented freezer, grew it to two routes and sold them.
ideas.business_model: Wholesale resale of packaged pastries to retail stores, then sale of the routes as assets.
ideas.customer: Gas stations, grocery and convenience stores
ideas.problem: The previous owner was a bad operator who hired badly and wanted passive income.
ideas.offer: Resell Bone Appetit danishes and donuts to stores, service them directly.

pricing.model: Resale margin of about $0.40 net per donut
pricing.notes: Shelf life and outdated returns were a pain.

acquisition_channels.details: Went to existing stores, introduced himself as the new route operator.

ideas.delivery: Shipped from a California bakery, rented freezer space in Colorado, delivered by van to stores himself and with his wife.
unit_economics_claims: Bought at $15k when it grossed about $100k and netted about $30-40k
Grew to about $800k gross in about two years with about $180k profit
Sold his wife's route with van for $85k and his route for $100k

uk_applicability.notes: Packaged baked goods distribution exists in the UK, but short shelf life, hygiene rules and incumbents like big bakery brands apply.

risks: Dependence on the bakery, which could pull the plug

ideas.name: Startup beverage brand distribution sales (employee)
ideas.one_liner: Forest grew a magnesium/CBD beverage brand from zero accounts to hundreds across Colorado by selling to regional accounts first and then signing distributors.
ideas.business_model: Salaried brand sales role (with small equity stake)
ideas.problem: New brands cannot get distributors without proven sales.
ideas.offer: Prove sales through independent and regional accounts, then hand to distributors.

acquisition_channels.details: Knocked on store doors, built hundreds of accounts, opened about eight distributors in Colorado.

uk_applicability.notes: The bottoms-up proof-then-distributor approach works the same in the UK.

ideas.name: Novelty-goods traveling route (retired couple)
ideas.one_liner: A 60-65 year old couple travel in a camper selling novelty items (shot glasses, knives, t-shirts, fishing hooks) to stores, dropping a few thousand dollars of stock every couple of months.

acquisition_channels.details: Travel to stores and sell directly.

uk_applicability.notes: Gift and tourist shops exist in the UK, but the market is smaller.

ideas.name: Niche distribution to coffee shops and restaurants (syrups, straws, napkins)
ideas.one_liner: Forest notes the same route model can supply syrups to coffee shops or straws and napkins to restaurants.

uk_applicability.notes: Catering supply is a mature UK market.

ideas.name: Vending machine business (comparison)
ideas.one_liner: Host argues the route model is better than vending machines, which need $3,000 machines, $1,000 card readers, restocking and location testing.
unit_economics_claims: Forest says vending operators restock about every four months and make about $200

uk_applicability.notes: Vending is common in the UK.

tactics.name: Source products distributors cannot get (local and regional brands)
steps: Call competitors and local producers to learn what sells in the area
Google for interesting jerky or candy brands not yet in local distribution
Ask if they already have distribution in your area, and drop them if they do
Prioritise local brands: big wholesalers ignore them
Use a list of about 50 independent stores as proof when pitching brands

quote.text: My number one selling jerky is local out of Billings.
quote.speaker: Forest

tactics.name: No-risk merchandising offer
steps: Position as an addition to the store's existing wholesaler, not a replacement
Offer to place orders, stock and rotate the shelf every other week
Promise to buy back unsold items
Start with one item then expand into a full section

quote.text: I'm not taking over theirs. I'm just an addition to.
quote.speaker: Forest

tactics.name: Cash-flow structure with positive conversion cycle
steps: Get manufacturer terms net-14 to net-30
Give customers net-10, visiting every 14 days so you collect before the next delivery
Plough every dollar of early sales into new accounts and topping up stock

quote.text: most of them I have them on net 10.
quote.speaker: Forest

tactics.name: First account playbook
steps: Carry stock in the vehicle so you can close on the spot
Bring a price sheet and a one-page fun-facts flyer with photos
Expect several nos; re-visit on a fixed day every other week
Win on the second follow-up
Use independent-looking stores found on Google Maps, ignoring fuel brand

quote.text: I kept following up every other Tuesday even if I sold them anything or not.
quote.speaker: Forest

tactics.name: Outsourced receiving at a staffed storage facility
steps: Call local storage facilities that have on-site employees
Have staff receive and check pallet deliveries
Pay a little extra to avoid being on site
Dedicate Monday to warehouse and restocking

warnings.warning: Buying a business without real numbers is risky; owners who hire out without learning the operation fail
Markup and margin are not the same; a 50% markup is a 33% margin

lessons.lesson: Prove sales bottoms-up (independent accounts first) before approaching distributors or big buyers.
Win by being different: local or regional products avoid price competition with giants.
Buying a distressed small business from a bad operator can be a cheap education and a profitable asset.
Working in an industry as an employee gives you contacts and knowledge to start your own version.
Positive cash conversion (collect in 10 days, pay in 14-30) lets you start with almost no capital.
Take the burden off the buyer (ordering, inventory risk, buy-backs) to make the offer a no-brainer.
Business owners tend to help other business owners; call competitors in other regions for insight.
Learn the work before outsourcing it; the previous owner lost value by hiring out something he did not understand.
Do it and test small; if a product fails with a store you simply do not repeat it.
Sell your authentic story even without industry experience.
Physical, sweaty businesses face less AI-driven competition, but they also cap how far agents can automate them.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with specific, mostly consistent numbers and process detail, but revenue, margins and the pastry history are unverified self-reports with a short (about 16-month) track record. The host extrapolates hypothetical figures ($240k profit, $12M) and the 'better than vending' comparison is opinion.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Forest runs a YouTube channel and a paid Skool-style community teaching the business; the host sells the TK Owners community and promotes Beehiiv (sponsor read).
